claims.text: An ML interatomic-potential framework integrated with high-throughput molecular dynamics can predict melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties for high-entropy alloys.
The ML-IAP can be calibrated using ab-initio calculations and targeted experimental data.
The initial solid high-entropy alloys exhibit established short-range chemical order.
A physically informed ML-IAP can capture local atomic arrangements and short-range chemical ordering in multicomponent alloys.
Local atomic arrangement and short-range chemical order govern melting-transition behavior.
The machine-learned potential encodes the detailed interatomic interactions of the multicomponent system.
Molecular-dynamics trajectories generated by the ML-IAP yield accurate response functions across the melting transition.
Thermodynamic integration can accurately quantify changes in energy, entropy, and volume across melting.
Short-range ordering captured by the ML model determines the nucleation and progression of melting.
The method is expected to predict melting temperatures within ±10–15 K of experiment.
The method is expected to predict fusion enthalpy within ±10% of experiment.
The method will accurately quantify fusion entropy and volume change at melting.
The proposed method is more efficient than traditional empirical-potential approaches.
Traditional empirical-potential approaches often exhibit errors exceeding 20% in high-entropy systems.
Empirical or semi-empirical potentials not calibrated for high-entropy-alloy compositional complexity typically have larger errors and poor transferability.
Strong ordering or decomposition can limit the applicability of the proposed approach.
Unrepresented long-range interactions, including magnetic effects, can limit the applicability of the approach.
Applicability across the complete high-entropy-alloy composition space has not been established.
Independent experiments across diverse alloy compositions can test the proposed predictive performance.
Consistent errors greater than 15 K in melting temperature or greater than 10% in fusion enthalpy across a statistically significant number of compositions would falsify the approach.
